title: Choose U.S. or Global Stock Exposure
meta_description: Compare S&P 500 and global stock exposure through index scope, concentration, currency, tax, fund structure, rebalancing and investor behaviour.

sections.heading: The Choice Is About Exposure, Not the Next Winner
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows people studying a live market chart on a laptop. That is the temptation behind “S&P 500 or global?”: turn a long-term portfolio design question into a forecast about which line rises next. A sound choice starts instead with what each index owns, omits and concentrates.

The S&P 500 represents large companies listed in the United States under its eligibility and committee methodology. A broad global index can include the United States plus developed and emerging markets, while an ex-U.S. index deliberately removes U.S. stocks. These are different exposure sets, not interchangeable brands.

There is no universally correct winner. An investor’s residence, tax system, currency of future spending, existing pension, employment, property, time horizon and ability to stay invested all matter. A U.S. resident choosing a U.S. index faces a different household balance sheet from an Indian or UK investor buying the same fund.

Separate expected return from reliability of prediction. Recent performance, economic news and company quality may influence prices, but widely known strengths are not free. A portfolio should remain workable if the favoured region underperforms for years.

Define the decision before comparing funds: choose a strategic equity geography, choose a benchmark that expresses it, then choose an investable fund. Starting with the cheapest familiar ticker can make the product decide the policy accidentally.

This is education, not a personal recommendation. Stocks can fall sharply, currencies move and tax rules differ. Use regulated advice where needed and verify product documents, jurisdiction and account treatment before investing.

Frame the decision in percentages of total investable assets, not in fund count. A household with half its wealth in employer shares and half in a global fund is not simply “globally diversified.” Include pensions and restricted holdings where data is available, then identify which exposures the new contribution can actually change.

State the decision horizon. Money needed in five years may not belong in either equity choice, while retirement contributions intended for decades can tolerate different variation. Do not solve an asset-allocation problem by debating geography alone. First establish emergency cash, near-term liabilities and the amount that can remain exposed through a severe decline.

sections.heading: Name the Index Before Debating It
paragraphs: “Global” is ambiguous. A world index may cover developed markets only; an all-country index may add emerging markets; an all-cap index may include large, mid and small companies; a global ex-U.S. index omits the United States. Read the methodology and factsheet rather than relying on a fund name.

The [[S1|S&P U.S. indices methodology]] sets eligibility, float adjustment and constituent rules for the S&P 500 family. It is designed as a U.S. large-cap benchmark, not as a complete map of every public company or every country’s opportunity set.

The [[S2|MSCI ACWI index page]] and [[S3|FTSE Global Equity Index Series]] describe prominent global frameworks. Their country classification, coverage targets, review schedules and constituent counts can differ. Two products labelled global can therefore hold different markets and weights.

Distinguish an index from a fund. An index is a rules-based measurement; an ETF or mutual fund attempts to track it after fees, taxes, trading and operational choices. Several funds can follow the same benchmark with different costs, domicile, liquidity and securities-lending policies.

Record the benchmark’s full name, provider, market-cap segment, countries, rebalancing schedule and treatment of foreign ownership. Save the current factsheet and fund prospectus. Index providers can change methodology and country classification over a multi-decade holding period.

Use a plain-language holdings test. Can you explain what is missing? An S&P 500 fund omits non-U.S.-listed equities and most smaller U.S. companies. A developed-world fund omits emerging markets. A global ex-U.S. fund requires a separate U.S. allocation if worldwide exposure is the goal.

Confirm whether the benchmark uses the provider’s country classification or the company’s incorporation, listing, headquarters or operations. Providers can assign the same security differently under their rules. A precise index name is therefore more useful than debating whether one multinational feels American, British, Chinese or global.

sections.heading: Understand What U.S. Large-Cap Exposure Buys
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows the New York Stock Exchange covered by U.S. flags. It makes the S&P side of the comparison unmistakable: this is exposure to a specific national listing and governance ecosystem, even when constituent companies sell products around the world.

The S&P 500 offers one-fund access to many large, profitable U.S. businesses across sectors. It is widely tracked, liquid and available through low-cost products. Those are meaningful implementation advantages, especially where local accounts and tax rules favour domestic funds.

It is not equally weighted by company. A market-cap-weighted index allocates more to companies with larger float-adjusted values. When a small group becomes very large, their returns have more influence. Diversifying across 500 names does not mean each contributes one five-hundredth of risk.

Revenue outside the United States does not transform a U.S. index into a global equity allocation. A multinational still has its primary listing, legal environment, accounting, sector profile and valuation within the U.S. market. Foreign sales add business reach, not ownership of foreign-listed markets.

The index also changes. Companies enter and leave as eligibility and market values evolve. An investor receives the current large-cap U.S. market selected by the methodology, not a fixed collection of famous names purchased forever.

Ask whether other household assets already lean toward the United States. Employer shares, stock compensation, technology-sector employment, pension holdings and property exposure can make an additional U.S.-only fund less diversifying than it appears when viewed alone.

Recognise that large-cap quality and past resilience can attract capital until expectations become demanding. This does not predict a fall; it explains why admired businesses and attractive future returns are separate questions. The index is a systematic exposure, not a certificate that every current constituent is cheaply priced.

sections.heading: Understand What Broad Global Exposure Buys
paragraphs: The late photograph shows coins from many countries and currencies. It makes the global principle visible: ownership is spread across different markets rather than assuming one national market must remain dominant throughout the investor’s entire horizon.

A market-cap-weighted global index normally still assigns a large weight to U.S. companies when the U.S. market is large. Choosing global does not mean betting against America or dividing money equally among flags. It means allowing the eligible world market to set country weights under the index rules.

Global exposure adds foreign-listed companies, different sector mixes, economic cycles, currencies and policy environments. It also introduces withholding taxes, settlement differences, governance risks and markets that may underperform. Diversification spreads uncertainty; it does not remove it.

Country weights change as prices, issuance, free float and classification change. A global investor does not need to forecast which country replaces a leader. The index automatically increases markets that become more valuable and decreases those that become less valuable, subject to its methodology.

Coverage still has limits. Some markets restrict foreign investors; private companies are absent; small or frontier markets may be omitted; sanctions and capital controls can intervene. Global is broad, not literally every productive asset on Earth.

Check whether the fund includes the investor’s home market. A global all-country fund usually does; an ex-home or ex-U.S. product does not. Combining pieces requires intentional weights and rebalancing so the portfolio does not drift into an accidental regional bet.

A global benchmark also imports whatever the world market currently values most. It is not an equal-risk portfolio and does not deliberately buy the cheapest country. Investors who want equal country weights, factor tilts or valuation rules are choosing a different strategy that needs separate evidence, cost and behavioural analysis.

sections.heading: Measure Concentration at More Than One Level
paragraphs: Count companies, then examine weight. A portfolio can hold thousands of securities while its top companies, sectors or countries determine much of the movement. Review top-ten weight, largest sector, largest country and overlap with other accounts.

Look through funds to household exposures. Owning an S&P 500 fund, a Nasdaq-oriented fund, a technology fund and employer stock may repeat many of the same companies. Four ticker symbols can be one concentrated economic position.

Country concentration is not automatically wrong. A domestic allocation may match liabilities, tax benefits or available plans. The issue is whether the amount is deliberate, understood and tolerable under a long period of relative underperformance.

Sector balance matters because national markets differ structurally. One country may contain more technology and communication companies; another more financials, industrials or resources. A country decision can therefore become an unspoken sector decision.

Use a stress case rather than a slogan. Model a large-company decline, a technology drawdown, a weak dollar or strong home currency, and ten years of foreign leadership. Ask whether contributions and rebalancing would continue under each case.

Set concentration limits in the investment policy. Limits can apply to employer stock, any one fund, one country outside the benchmark or thematic positions. Review them on a schedule rather than after a headline makes the concentration uncomfortable.

Calculate overlap with constituent weights rather than only matching names. If one fund assigns eight percent to a company and another assigns five, the combined household weight depends on dollars invested in each. Use current holdings files and accept that the result changes as funds rebalance.

Concentration can hide in benchmark design as well as holdings. Profitability screens, listing requirements and committee discretion may produce a different company set from a total-market index. Read what the index is intended to measure, because a well-known name does not guarantee exposure to every listed U.S. company or every source of economic growth.

sections.heading: Do Not Count Multinational Revenue as Full Diversification
paragraphs: A common argument says U.S. multinationals earn abroad, so investors already own the world. Foreign revenue can diversify customer demand, but revenue geography is only one dimension. Listing, valuation, shareholder rights, sector composition and access to foreign firms remain concentrated.

A company can sell globally while its stock reacts to U.S. rates, regulation, index flows and domestic investor sentiment. A foreign company can also earn substantial U.S. revenue. Sales location and security domicile answer different questions.

Revenue data is inconsistent across companies and changes over time. Firms report regions differently, and supply chains, costs and taxes may not align with customer location. Do not build precise geographic weights from a rough marketing statistic.

Direct foreign holdings provide access to companies and industries not represented at the same weight in the S&P 500. They also add risks specific to those markets. The purpose is not purity; it is broader sources of return and governance exposure.

Use a four-column look-through: listing country, revenue regions, operating assets and currency sensitivity. No single column defines exposure, but together they reveal why a multinational is not a substitute for an entire foreign market.

Treat multinational reach as a feature of U.S. large caps, not a reason to stop analysing country concentration. The strategic question remains whether the investor wants only U.S.-listed large companies or a broader ownership set.

Distinguish diversification of revenue from diversification of security pricing. Two firms serving the same global customer base may still react differently because they face different regulators, shareholder bases, financing markets and sector weights. Direct international ownership adds those pricing systems; it does not guarantee that correlations remain low in a crisis.

sections.heading: Separate Currency Noise From Equity Risk
paragraphs: An unhedged foreign holding changes value with both the local security and exchange rate relative to the investor’s reporting currency. Currency can raise or lower returns over a period. The effect is not an extra coupon; it is another source of variation.

Identify the currency of future liabilities. Someone expecting retirement spending in pounds, dollars or rupees may reasonably view the same global fund differently. Yet company cash flows are international, so listing currency alone does not reveal complete economic currency exposure.

Currency hedging can reduce some exchange-rate movement, but it has cost, implementation and tax consequences. Hedged and unhedged share classes can track different benchmarks. Read the policy rather than assuming a fund’s trading currency determines whether currency is hedged.

Do not switch geography after a dramatic currency move merely to chase the recent winner. Rebalancing rules should specify whether exchange-rate changes are allowed to move weights and when trades occur.

For long horizons, equities and currencies interact in complicated ways. Avoid claims that currency always washes out or always dominates. Model outcomes in the currency of the goal and keep assumptions visible.

Cash and bonds may be better tools for near-term currency matching than forcing the equity portfolio to do every job. Separate short-term spending reserves from long-term growth assets before deciding the geographic equity mix.

If a fund offers several currency share classes, compare the benchmark and hedge policy line by line. A dollar ticker can own unhedged Japanese and European stocks; a sterling-traded class can do the same. Trading currency mainly describes the unit used to buy and quote the fund, not all underlying risks.

sections.heading: Past Leadership Is Not a Portfolio Policy
paragraphs: Regional leadership rotates. A chart beginning at a favourable date can make either U.S. or international stocks look inevitable. Examine multiple start dates, valuation regimes and currency environments instead of one trailing return window.

Strong fundamentals do not guarantee strong future returns when expectations are already reflected in price. Weak recent performance does not guarantee a rebound. Valuation can inform expectations, but it is not a reliable short-term timing signal.

Avoid the historical-average trap. Markets, index composition, taxes and accounting evolve. A backtest shows what a rule would have done under recorded conditions, not what the next sequence must deliver.

Include the path, not just ending wealth. Two allocations can reach similar long-term outcomes with different drawdowns and decade-long relative performance. The investable policy is the one the household can continue funding during an uncomfortable path.

Test regret in both directions. How would the investor respond if the U.S. led for another decade after choosing global? How would they respond if foreign markets led after choosing U.S. only? A robust allocation limits the temptation to abandon the plan under either result.

Write the reason for every tilt before seeing its result. “Recent outperformance” and “this country is obviously the future” are weak reasons because they change with prices. Tax, liabilities, access and a bounded risk preference are more durable.

Beware return comparisons that mix gross index, net index and fund returns. Withholding assumptions, fees, tracking and reinvestment timing can create differences unrelated to geographic skill. Compare consistent return types, currencies and dates, and preserve the source so the chart can be reproduced later.

sections.heading: Home Bias Can Be Useful or Accidental
paragraphs: Home bias means holding more domestic equity than its share of a chosen global benchmark. It can arise from familiarity, workplace plans, tax advantages, lower fees, currency comfort or confidence in local institutions. Some reasons are practical; familiarity alone is not diversification.

Map the whole household balance sheet. Salary, public benefits, property, business ownership and career prospects often depend on the home economy even when the securities portfolio does not. More domestic stocks can compound that common exposure.

Tax-advantaged accounts may offer a limited menu or preferential domestic treatment. Use the best available account without pretending its menu defines ideal global allocation. Other accounts can fill gaps when costs and rules permit.

Non-U.S. investors should not treat an S&P 500 fund as domestic. They take U.S. equity exposure plus cross-border fund, currency, estate, withholding and regulatory considerations determined by domicile and treaties. The ticker’s trading venue does not settle these issues.

Set a range rather than a perfect percentage. A global benchmark can anchor the neutral position; a documented home tilt can reflect real constraints. The range reduces needless trading as market weights move.
Review home bias when residence, citizenship, employment, pension or future spending currency changes. A policy inherited from a previous country or job may no longer match the household.

Home bias can also reduce a mismatch when liabilities, taxes and access are strongly domestic. The decision is not a contest between sophistication and provincialism. Quantify the practical benefit, set a maximum and examine household concentration; a bounded tilt is different from assuming the familiar market cannot disappoint.

sections.heading: Choose the Fund Only After Choosing the Exposure
paragraphs: Compare benchmark, domicile, replication, ongoing fee, tracking difference, spreads, fund size, securities lending, income treatment and tax reporting. A tiny fee difference should not distract from the wrong index or an unsuitable legal structure.

Accumulating and distributing share classes handle income differently. They do not erase tax obligations. Confirm reporting and account treatment in the investor’s jurisdiction, especially for cross-border funds.

Physical replication may hold all or a sample of securities; synthetic replication uses derivatives and collateral. Neither label alone decides suitability. Read how the fund achieves exposure and what counterparty or sampling risks remain.

Use limit orders and liquid trading hours where appropriate, but avoid turning a long-term allocation into frequent execution optimisation. Spreads and premiums can widen when underlying markets are closed or stressed.

Check closure, merger and index-change procedures. A fund can be low cost and still create inconvenience or a taxable event if it closes. Larger established products may reduce some operational risk but do not guarantee continuity.

Verify through official documents and regulated platforms. Investor.gov explains [[S5|index funds]] and [[S4|diversification]] at a consumer level. Marketing rankings and social posts are discovery tools, not due diligence.

Review the product’s authorised participant, market-maker and custody arrangements at the level appropriate for the investor. Most households do not need to engineer every operational detail, but they should understand that an ETF’s exchange price, net asset value and underlying-market liquidity are related yet distinct during stress.

Before buying, confirm the exact security identifier and exchange. Similar names can refer to different share classes, currencies, distributing policies or domiciles. Save the key investor document and prospectus from the provider. A screenshot from a brokerage search is not a durable explanation of what the household owns.

sections.heading: Taxes Can Reverse a Superficial Comparison
paragraphs: Tax depends on residence, account, fund domicile, security type, income, treaty and holding period. Two investors buying economically similar exposure may receive different net results. Never copy a product choice across borders without checking the structure.

Foreign dividends may face withholding before reaching the fund or investor. Some leakage can be recovered or credited; some cannot. The result depends on layers in the holding chain and the account used.

Capital-gains rules can make rebalancing costly in taxable accounts. New contributions, dividends and tax-advantaged accounts may restore weights with fewer realised gains. Keep records of cost basis and elections as required.

Estate and inheritance rules can create consequences unrelated to annual fund fees. Cross-border investors should seek qualified advice where U.S.-situs or other foreign assets may trigger filing or tax exposure.

Do not let tax efficiency justify a poor overall allocation, but compare after-tax, after-fee outcomes. A slightly higher-cost fund with suitable domicile or reporting may be better than the headline cheapest product.
Rules change. Record the advice date, assumptions and official sources. Recheck after moving country, changing account type, marrying, inheriting or approaching withdrawals.

Model tax drag over the intended holding period rather than comparing one year in isolation. Dividend yield, turnover, withholding and realisation policy influence compounding. Estimates should use conservative assumptions and be checked by a qualified adviser when the product crosses jurisdictions or the account has special status.

sections.heading: Rebalance Without Forecasting the Next Region
paragraphs: Choose calendar, threshold or contribution-based rebalancing. Calendar review checks weights on a fixed date; thresholds act after drift; contributions direct new money toward the underweight area. The policy should specify method and allowable ranges.

A single global market-cap fund rebalances country weights internally as the benchmark changes. A U.S.-plus-ex-U.S. portfolio requires the investor to maintain the chosen split, but may offer tax or product flexibility.
Rebalancing sells some relative winners and buys relative laggards to restore risk policy. It is not a promise of higher return. Costs, taxes and minimum trade sizes can justify tolerance bands.
Track all accounts together. Rebalancing each account in isolation can create unnecessary trades while the household total is already on target. Respect account restrictions and withdrawal timing.

Do not rebalance in response to commentary unless the policy trigger is met or circumstances changed. Headlines are not a separate asset-allocation rule. If the strategic target changes, write the new reason before trading.
Keep records of target, actual weight, trade, cost and tax consequence. A short annual log makes later performance understandable and prevents memory from rewriting the decision.

For threshold rebalancing, define the threshold as percentage points or a relative deviation and use it consistently. A five-point drift from 60% to 65% is different from a five-percent relative change. Ambiguous rules invite market opinions to decide whether a trade supposedly qualifies.

sections.heading: Design for the Behavioural Failure Point
paragraphs: The hardest allocation is not the one with the lowest projected return; it is the one abandoned after relative underperformance. A globally diversified investor may resent foreign holdings when U.S. stocks lead. A U.S.-only investor may chase foreign markets after leadership changes.

Reduce comparison noise. Compare the portfolio with its policy benchmark, not whichever index won this year. A global allocation will rarely beat the best country in any period because it owns the laggards too; that is the cost of not needing to identify the winner in advance.

Automate contributions and limit review frequency. Daily performance checks make normal divergence feel like a decision emergency. Quarterly or annual policy review is usually enough for a long-term geographic allocation.

Write a bear-market instruction: continue scheduled contributions if the funding plan remains sound, check cash needs, rebalance only under the rule and do not sell solely because prices fell. Personal circumstances can still justify change.

Use a small bounded tilt if it prevents a larger behavioural mistake. An investor strongly convinced about U.S. leadership might hold global as the core and a limited U.S. tilt, with an explicit maximum. The compromise must remain simpler than the conflict it solves.

Discuss the plan with affected household members. A portfolio that one partner does not understand can fail during stress. Explain ownership, expected differences, drawdowns and who may authorise changes.

Keep performance reporting aligned with contribution timing. Money-weighted return reflects the household’s cash flows, while time-weighted return helps compare management of the allocation. Neither measure alone proves that one geography decision was wise; contributions and market sequence can dominate a short evaluation period.

sections.heading: Write the Geography Policy in One Page
paragraphs: State the objective, equity percentage, geographic benchmark, any home or U.S. tilt, allowed ranges, accounts, contribution order and rebalancing rule. Name the evidence that could justify change, such as residence or tax status—not recent returns.
List deliberate omissions. If emerging markets, small caps or the home market are excluded, say why. Unwritten omissions are difficult to distinguish from oversight when reviewing years later.
Add an overlap check and concentration limits. Record employer stock, sector funds and other holdings that repeat benchmark constituents. Set the maximum for positions outside the core.

Include implementation facts: fund legal name, identifier, benchmark, domicile, share class, fee, income treatment and document date. Tickers can be reused across exchanges and are not enough for permanent records.
Review annually and after major life changes, not after every market rotation. Update factsheets and tax assumptions while preserving the strategic reason unless circumstances genuinely changed.

The final test is simple: can the investor explain what is owned, what is missing, why the geography fits household risks and what happens when the other choice wins for years? If yes, either a U.S.-focused or broad global policy can be deliberate. If not, more forecasting will not repair the missing design.

Add a decision hierarchy: first confirm goal and stock capacity, then geographic benchmark, then tilts, then fund and account, and only then trade. Reversing the hierarchy encourages product availability or a popular ticker to determine risk. The one-page policy should make this order visible to every authorised decision-maker.

Record who can amend the policy and how disagreement is resolved. A partner should not discover during a drawdown that one person considered the allocation temporary. Requiring a cooling period, updated household facts and written approval makes strategic changes slower than emotional trades while still allowing necessary action after a genuine life change. Keep the signed record with the household investment documents and review calendar. Preserve it securely.

summary: The S&P 500 versus global decision is about exposure, not forecasting the next winner. Define household residence, taxes, future spending currency, existing assets, horizon and ability to remain invested before selecting an index or fund.

Name the benchmark precisely. S&P 500 is U.S. large-cap exposure; developed world, all-country, all-cap and ex-U.S. indices include different markets and company sizes. An index sets rules, while a fund tracks it with fees, taxes and operational differences.

S&P 500 funds offer liquid, low-cost access to major U.S. companies, but market-cap weighting can concentrate influence in the largest names and sectors. Foreign revenue does not convert U.S.-listed companies into full foreign-market ownership.

Broad global indices usually retain a large U.S. allocation while adding foreign-listed companies, sector mixes, currencies and policy environments. They remain incomplete and introduce their own tax, governance and market risks.

Measure concentration by weight, country, sector and overlap across all household accounts. Multiple funds may repeat the same companies. Stress-test large-company declines, regional leadership changes and currency moves rather than relying on security count.

Currency affects unhedged foreign returns, but listing currency is not full economic exposure. Match near-term spending with suitable cash or bonds and decide separately whether equity currency hedging fits costs and goals.

Do not turn recent regional leadership into policy. Examine several periods and paths, test regret in both directions and document tilts before their results are known. Valuation informs expectations but does not provide reliable short-term timing.

Home bias may reflect tax, available plans, liabilities or familiarity. Map salary, pension, property and business exposure because domestic stocks can compound risks already tied to the home economy. Non-U.S. investors face cross-border issues when buying U.S. funds.

Choose exposure before product. Compare benchmark, domicile, replication, tracking difference, spreads, securities lending, income treatment and tax reporting. Verify official documents and regulated platforms rather than selecting from rankings or social posts.

Compare after-tax, after-fee outcomes. Withholding, account rules, cost basis, estate exposure and treaties can make similar portfolios behave differently. Recheck advice after moves, inheritance, marriage or withdrawal changes.

Rebalance by calendar, threshold or contributions under written ranges. Track all accounts together and record costs and taxes. A global single fund adjusts country weights internally; separate U.S. and ex-U.S. funds require deliberate maintenance.

Design for relative underperformance. Compare with the policy benchmark, automate contributions, limit review and write a bear-market instruction. A bounded tilt may be acceptable when it prevents a larger behaviour failure.
Write a one-page geography policy with objective, benchmark, ranges, omissions, overlap limits, account placement, funds and review date. Recent returns alone never justify a strategic change.

The usable allocation is one the investor can explain and hold when the alternative leads for years. Either U.S.-focused or broad global exposure can be deliberate; neither removes loss, uncertainty or the need to understand what is missing.

Evaluate exposure in household dollars, not ticker count. Include employer shares, pensions and repeated constituents, and calculate overlap using actual weights. Precise benchmark methodology matters because providers differ in country classification, eligibility, free float and market coverage.

Compare like with like: gross versus net index returns, fund returns after fees, common currencies, dates and reinvestment assumptions. Distinguish trading currency from hedging, and model dividend withholding and tax drag over the intended holding period rather than one convenient year.

Use a decision hierarchy: goal and stock capacity first, geographic benchmark second, bounded tilts third, product and account fourth, trade last. Define rebalance thresholds unambiguously and keep performance measurement consistent with contribution timing so short sequences do not rewrite the policy.

faq.question: Is the S&P 500 already globally diversified because companies sell overseas?
faq.answer: Foreign revenue broadens customer exposure, but the index remains U.S.-listed large-cap equity with its own country, sector, valuation and governance concentration.

faq.question: Does a global index exclude the United States?
faq.answer: Usually not. Broad all-country indices generally include the United States at a market-cap weight. An ex-U.S. index explicitly removes it.

faq.question: Is more companies always more diversified?
faq.answer: No. Examine weights, sectors, countries and overlap across all accounts. Thousands of holdings can still be dominated by a small group of companies or one country.

faq.question: Should international equity currency be hedged?
faq.answer: It depends on goal currency, horizon, cost, product and tax treatment. Fund trading currency does not itself determine whether underlying exposure is hedged.

faq.question: Can recent performance identify the better allocation?
faq.answer: No. Leadership rotates and start dates alter comparisons. A strategic policy should remain workable through years when the other region leads.

faq.question: Can U.S. and ex-U.S. funds be combined instead of using one global fund?
faq.answer: Yes, but the investor must choose the split, place funds across accounts and rebalance. A single global fund maintains benchmark country weights internally.

faq.question: What should trigger a policy change?
faq.answer: A material change in residence, taxes, liabilities, access, household risk or goals may justify review. Recent market performance alone should not.

glossary.definition: An index of large U.S. companies selected and weighted under S&P Dow Jones Indices methodology.
A benchmark covering eligible developed and emerging equity markets.
An international equity benchmark that intentionally excludes U.S. securities.
Weighting securities according to eligible market value so larger companies receive larger positions.
Shares considered available to public investors after relevant ownership restrictions.
Holding more domestic equity than its weight in a chosen global benchmark.
The return gap between a fund and its benchmark after fees and implementation effects.
The legal jurisdiction where an investment fund is established.
Using instruments intended to reduce specified exchange-rate effects.
Restoring portfolio weights toward policy targets under a defined rule.
